subject: psychiatry
title: Delirium

steps.tx: **Delirium** is acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with cognitive change developing over hours to days from medical causes, distinct from dementia (chronic, attention preserved early) though delirium superimposed on dementia is commonest hospital reality. Hypoactive delirium (quiet, withdrawn, drowsy) is missed most and carries worst outcomes; hyperactive agitation draws attention; mixed forms fluctuate. Every delirium is medical emergency workup: infection, hypoxia, metabolic, drugs, withdrawal, pain, retention and intracranial causes via structured bundles (TIME, PINCH ME patterns).
steps.say: Acute confused and inattentive means delirium until cause found. Quiet hypoactive delirium kills most and is missed most.

steps.tx: Diagnosis uses **CAM** logic: acute fluctuating course plus inattention, plus either disorganised thinking or altered consciousness. Collateral history establishes baseline and acuity; examination seeks infection source, dehydration, drug culprits (anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines), withdrawal states and focal neurology. Investigations follow clues: observations, glucose, bloods, cultures, ECG, imaging only with focal signs, trauma or failure to improve.
steps.say: CAM needs acute fluctuation plus inattention plus messy thinking or consciousness. History from family proves acuity.

steps.tx: Management treats causes, not just behaviour: **HELP** style multicomponent prevention (orientation, hydration, early mobilisation, sleep hygiene, glasses and hearing aids, pain control) prevents a third of hospital delirium. Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium generally and are reserved low dose short term for severe distress or danger unresponsive to de escalation (cautions in Parkinson and Lewy body where sensitivity can be lethal, favouring quetiapine class specialist choices or none). Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium where they are treatment. Restraint and catheters aggravate it.
steps.say: Prevent with orientation, water, movement, sleep and spectacles. Antipsychotics only for danger, never routine. Benzodiazepines worsen unless withdrawal.

steps.tx: **Key point.** Prognosis is grave beyond the ward: delirium multiplies mortality, institutionalisation and later dementia risk, so discharge needs cognitive follow up and family explanation that recovery can take weeks to months. Persistent delirium demands re hunt for occult infection, subdural, autoimmune or non convulsive seizures (EEG). Capacity fluctuates with delirium, so major decisions wait or use legal frameworks with reassessment.
steps.say: Delirium scars brains long term: survivors need cognitive follow up. Decisions wait for clear days where possible.
